WATER SAFETY DURING COLD WEATHER  
 
Our Water Safety Office issued a public advisory in November on 
Water Safety specifically during Cold Weather. Cold winter 
waters can cause “cold shock” and hypothermia which can set in 
within a short period of time. This is especially so if there is a 
high wind chill factor which can overwhelm even the fittest of 
swimmers. 
Member of the Public are urged to prepare for a winter swim 
following the below guidance issued through our Social Media 
channels:  
• Immediately before the swim, people should throw cold water on themselves and 
always ease into the water slowly introducing your body to the low temperature. 
• Check local weather forecasts and tides to avoid drowning risks such as rip currents 
or hypothermia. 
• Heed the advice of other seasoned swimmers. If they advise against swimming due 
to the conditions, then do not enter the water. 
• Stay in your depth – know your limits including how long to stay in the water and 
swim parallel to the shore. 
• If you get into trouble lean back in the water, extending your arms and legs, and 
resisting the urge to thrash around to gain control of your breathing. 
• Post-swim it is important to warm up as quickly as possible Be prepared with a dry 
towel, warm layers and a hot drink following your swim.

If you see a person in difficulty, do not attempt a rescue for which you are not trained. Make 
use of nearby public rescue equipment such as a ringbuoy.

Galway County Council championed the production of Mise Éire, a collaboration with 5th

Cathaoirleach of Galway

event’s impact.

By investing in local talent - teachers, adjudicators, film production student volunteers and

network of Irish language enthusiasts.

Scoil an Phiarsaigh 2025 now stands as a testament to Galway County Council’s vision for 
cultural renewal and linguistic vitality. By blending heritage with innovation this year 
specifically, the 2-day reimagined programme has created a dynamic platform where 
education, creativity, and community converge to make Irish a living language for all 
generations. 
 The event bolsters our strategic alignment with national policy but also a deep commitment

its leadership in shaping a future where language, identity, and community thrive together 
when we work together collaboratively across Directorates and with our communities.

LOCAL COMMUNITY SAFETY PARTNERSHIP (LCSP) 
 
A new statutory body focused on improving community safety in County Galway held its 
first meeting at Áras an Chontae on the 2nd December, marking the formal end of the Joint 
Policing Committee (JPC) model. 
The Galway County Local Community Safety Partnership (LCSP) has been set up under the 
Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024 as part of a national shift towards wider 
and more inclusive planning. Its members include up to 30 people from Galway County 
Council, An Garda Síochána, the HSE, Tusla and local organisations representing youth, 
social inclusion, education, business and community groups.

10 
 
Over the next three years the Partnership will draw up a safety plan for the county, 
coordinate new initiatives, engage with residents and feed into the work of the National 
Office for Community Safety. The National Office will offer training and support and will 
oversee the Community Safety Fund, which uses proceeds of crime to back local projects. 
  
During the first meeting, Cllr Andrew Reddington was elected Chair for a three-year term, 
and Aodán McDonogh was chosen as Vice Chair. 
  
Cllr Reddington commented, “Each area of County Galway has its own specific safety and 
community issues that no single organisation can solve alone. Real progress depends on 
various agencies working together, from policing to local government and health services, as 
well as community groups. We aim to unite these perspectives so local people can help 
guide how safety improves in County Galway." 
  
Vice Chairperson Aodán McDonogh emphasised that the Partnership strongly prioritises 
collaboration and places local voices at the heart of decision-making. 
  
Membership from the community and voluntary sector was confirmed through a 
nomination process led by the Chief Executive of Galway County Council. This was reviewed 
by the National Office and approved by Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Jim 
O'Callaghan TD. 
  
Welcoming members to the first meeting of the LCSP, Chief Executive Liam Conneally said 
the Partnership replaces the Joint Policing Committee (JPC) model and represents a new 
approach to local community safety.  
  
“The LCSP brings all the key agencies together to look at the safety issues affecting our 
communities and to agree practical actions to address them,” he said. “It gives local people 
a stronger voice in identifying priorities and helps ensure that services work in a more 
joined-up way. Galway County Council looks forward to working with other agencies in 
developing and overseeing a new Community Safety Plan for the county, focused on 
prevention, collaboration and improving quality of life for everyone who lives here.” 
  
The Partnership will meet at least six times a year. One of the meetings will be open to the 
public, while another will be for elected representatives from the Oireachtas and Galway 
County Council. 
  
It will also collaborate with neighbouring partnerships and existing local structures, 
including the Local Community Development Committee, Galway County Public 
Participation Network, and youth groups such as Comhairle na nÓg and the Children and 
Young People’s Services Committee. The LCSP will not address individual criminal 
investigations, State security matters, or confidential Garda operations.

WOMEN’S HEALTH PROGRAMME  
EVALUATION OF THE WOMEN’S HEALTH PROGRAMME – AUTUMN 5-WEEK TALK 
SERIES 
The evaluation of the most recent 
Women’s Health Programme, 
delivered as a five-week talk series in 
Autumn, provided valuable insights to 
inform the development of a tailored 
programme for 2026 that will reflect 
both stakeholder and participant feedback.

12 
 
Participants reported adopting a variety of positive practices following the sessions, 
including dietary improvements, increased physical activity, and mindfulness techniques. 
Examples shared included adding nutrient rich foods to their diet, using acupressure points, 
practicing yoga, and prioritising time for self-care mentally and physically. While some 
attendees experienced significant improvements in health and wellbeing, others noted 
gradual progress. Overall, the 
programme was credited with raising 
awareness and motivating lifestyle 
changes, with feedback highlighting the 
importance of early intervention and 
continued education. 
Suggestions for future programmes included tailoring sessions for older age groups, 
particularly women over 65 and 70+, with content such as chair yoga, osteoporosis-friendly 
exercises, and wellbeing strategies for later life. Participants also requested more mental 
health-focused sessions and practical demonstrations of home-based exercises using 
weights or resistance bands. There was a strong interest expressed in follow-up 
programmes, WhatsApp groups for ongoing updates, and in-person wellbeing activities such 
as Tai Chi, mindfulness, and meditation. Respondents further suggested further introductory 
sessions on weight-bearing exercises and to help 
demystify fitness for older women. 
Following on from this Healthy County Galway has 
been approached by the Technological University of 
the Shannon (TUS) to help generate interest among 
women in participating in a Women’s Wellness Testing 
Day. This research initiative focuses on 
postmenopausal women and aims to provide fitness 
and health assessments, including strength, flexibility, 
aerobic fitness, and body composition, alongside 
tailored exercise and nutrition guidance. 
The key role of Healthy County Galway will be to 
identify and engage partners who are interested in 
facilitating this screening in locations across County 
Galway and the offshore islands. This collaborative approach will ensure accessibility and 
inclusivity for women in rural and island communities in county Galway. There has already 
been strong interest expressed from groups in Connemara, the islands, and the HSE, 
highlighting the potential impact for women and reach of this initiative. 
Participants will benefit from immediate fitness results, a free online booklet with tailored 
exercise and nutrition tips, and the opportunity to contribute to research aimed at 
improving health supports for postmenopausal women.

CONNEMARA DEMENTIA CAFÉ INITIATIVE 
The Memory Café Initiative in Connemara is hosting a special 
Christmas social gathering to promote social connection among 
attendees and caregivers. This festive event will take place on 
Monday, 8th December at 12:30 pm in the Station House Hotel, 
Clifden, and will include Christmas lunch, carol singing, music, and 
song. The aim of this gathering is to strengthen community ties and 
welcome participants to explore other Memory Cafés in other 
locations around Connemara encouraging a wider network of 
support and engagement.  
This initiative continues to grow, with strong participation across Connemara. In particular, 
the most recently established Oughterard Memory Café has been very well attended and 
has offered a variety of enriching activities. These have included arts and crafts using activity 
packs, facilitated by Keelin Kennedy, and movement sessions through chair yoga, which

have been highly valued by attendees. These activities not only provide creative and 
physical stimulation but also contribute to the overall wellbeing and social inclusion of 
attendees with cognitive impairment and their caregivers.

RURAL DEVELOPMENT & VILLAGE RENEWAL - GRANTS SCHEME 
 
TOWN & VILLAGE RENEWAL SCHEME  
In November 2025 two main projects were completed under the 2023 Town and Village 
Renewal Scheme, representing an investment of over 600k in Community Facilities and the 
recoupment of 500k in grant aid from Department of Community, Rural Development and 
the Gaeltachta. Both facilities provide essential space for community groups and 
organisations, recreation, well-being and cultural events.  Working with these Committees a 
key issue arising is that, while capital investment is vital to maximise the use of these 
community assets, support is also needed to sustain their use including the continuation of 
employment schemes, social enterprise or other schemes to assist with the day-to-day 
caretaking and operation of the facilities which is handled by volunteers.   
DUNMORE TOWN HALL - COMPLETION OF €250,000 TVRS FUNDED INVESTMENT  
Dunmore Town Hall occupies a prominent corner site and is a Protected Structure, almost 
100 years old.  Further to community consultation and preliminary designs from Feeney 
McMahon Architects investment in the Town Hall under Town and Village, prioritised access 
and addressed the requirement for much needed upgrades to provide a comfortable 
accessible community space located within the heart of Dunmore Town centre. The project 
has addressed a deficit of available community space through improved building thermal 
performance and comfort for new daytime users as well as existing evening weekly and 
monthly community 
events – e.g. 25 Card 
game & Monster Bingo.  
The Hall, hosts Foróige, 
Parent and Toddler 
Groups and Active Age 
Activities as well as 
Cultural and Entertainment venue year-round and as a hub in the Annual Dunmore Festival.   
The Property is held in Trust for the Community by the Trustees of Dunmore Community 
and Leased to Dunmore Community Council. The delivery of the project was led by a sub-
group of Dunmore Community Council and there is a sense of pride in the achievement, 
which involved significant co-ordination and consultation with users of the hall suppliers 
and trades resulting in improved visual appearance and internal upgrades the Kitchen and 
Main Hall.  Total Expenditure was €264,392.79 with Grant Funding of 250,000.  The 
Community Council are proposed a formal re-launch event in early 2026 to include 
Members of the Tuam Municipal District.

MAREE COMMUNITY CENTRE - COMPLETION OF €250,000 TVRS FUNDED 
INVESTMENT 
The Maree Community Centre is a multi-use community facility, with indoor recreational 
space for functions, community meetings, family events, education and training, basketball 
court and gym adjacent to the National School.  Providing for the growing population in 
Maree and the rural hinterlands of Oranmore and beyond, it is a much used and in demand 
space which required critical upgrades and repairs.  The investment in this community asset 
was vital for the continued operation of the Maree Community Centre which had 
experienced leaks and damage to the roof.   
The project was driven by a sub-committee of Maree Community Development Association 
(MCDA) with support of local consulting engineers.  Initial works were reviewed post-
tender, and it was agreed with GCC and DRCDG given the estimated costs for all works to 
focus on the priority of a full roof replacement and roof insulation, which was delivered on 
time and within budget by this hard-working group of volunteers.  The delivery timeline was 
impacted by the availability of roofing contractors post Storm Eyown and working around 
the National School holidays to ensure safety.   The total expenditure was €263,356.00. This 
has improved energy efficiency and sustainability, which will impact on reducing heating 
costs and benefitting the environment.  Improved facilities will sustain its continued and 
safe use.

• Implement the Planning and Development Act 2024 to speed up planning.

Galway County Council has significant developments in tenancy management and housing

TENANCY MOVEMENTS AND HOUSING TRENDS 
2025 saw a clear trend toward Approved Housing Bodies (AHBs) who avail of RAS support, 
primarily through CAS-funded units designed for Older Persons Accommodation (OPA), 
Disability, and Homeless households. These AHB tenancies increased by 54 units during the 
year, reflecting Galway County Council’s strategic focus on long-term, sustainable housing 
solutions for vulnerable groups. 
In contrast, private RAS tenancies declined by 13 units, a natural outcome of transfers to 
other housing options and scheme exits. Private landlord participation also decreased 
slightly, from 98 to 88, indicating consolidation 
within the scheme. This mirrors a national 
trend of private landlords leaving the rental 
market, driven by regulatory changes, rising 
compliance costs, and market pressures. 
Galway County Council acknowledges this 
challenge and is actively working to retain and 
attract landlords to the RAS programme.

Maintaining quality housing standards remained a priority throughout 2025. Inspections 
were carried out regularly, with properties assessed for suitability under RAS guidelines.

welfare. Inspections were most active in January, April, and during the summer months, 
ensuring that properties met required standards before and during occupancy.

No vacant-unit claims were recorded during the year, and there were zero transfers to the 
Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) scheme. This stability reflects effective tenancy

The increase in AHB tenancies—primarily CAS-funded units for older persons, disability, and 
homelessness—demonstrates Galway County Council’s commitment to delivering secure, 
long-term homes through collaborative partnerships. This approach aligns with national 
housing policy and ensures that vulnerable households have access to quality 
accommodation. The Council’s strategy emphasises sustainability, affordability, and tenant 
security, positioning AHBs as key partners in meeting housing demand.

RAS continues to play a vital role in supporting families and individuals who require social

ROUTES COVERED 
The routes treated are categorised according to strategic importance as set out below. 
 
Priority 1 routes consist of Motorway, dual carriage way, national primary and secondary 
routes and include a number of sections of strategic regional route network.  These routes 
are ordinarily treated and receive precautionary treatment.  Every effort will be made to 
ensure that these routes are treated by 8.00 am in the morning.

but will be considered for treatment by the Duty Engineer once priority 1 & 2 routes are 
addressed and as resources allow at that time. 
  
Priority 4 routes are other local roads and footpaths and will not be considered for 
treatment except in severe or prolonged winter weather and then only when resources are 
available.

18km National Primary, 282km National Secondary and 928km Regional and Local Road.

554km.

TII have indicated that they are embarking on a programme to move to treating all national 
routes with pre-wet salt. Currently Galway County Council only engage in dry salt spreading 
and do not have the infrastructure carry out pre-wet spreading. Pre wet salting is 
considered a more efficient and effective method of treating roads, albeit involving a

installation of new public EV charging hubs and the upgrading of existing charger locations. 
 One of Zevi’s key goals, which is fully aligned with Climate Action Plan 2025 objectives, is to 
achieve a target of having 30% of Ireland's private car fleet be electric by 2030. 
Another notable ZEVI objective is to provide EV charging infrastructure (to include ultra-fast 
charging) for every 60km of motorway by 2030.

1. Neighbourhood charging - will provide for EV owners without access to a driveway. 
Charging hubs will be located in public spaces and will facilitate convenient slower 
off-peak EV charging 
2. Destination charging - will provide for EV charging while EV users are on the go or 
staying at a particular destination (shopping centre, hotel, tourist attraction).  These 
may be a combination of fast and ultra-fast charging points depending on user need. 
3. En-route charging - will provide for high power ultra-fast charge points at strategic 
locations, e.g. adjacent to Motorways. This will help address range anxiety.  
ZEVI has recently published a Regional and Local EV Charging Network Plan 2025-2030 from 
which Galway County Council is developing its own county-specific Local EV Charging 
Strategy and Plan.

HOLY WELLS AUDIT 2025 
The aim of the Audit of the Holy Wells of the County of Galway is to collect and collate 
information which may be in danger of being lost due to a largely, older generational 
knowledge base and land development pressures, including drainage and/or clearance. The 
data being collected through the County-wide audit of each holy well includes location, 
infrastructure, physical condition, access, protection status, ownership, archaeology, 
biodiversity, traditions, folklore, oral heritage and customs associated with and connected 
to the holy wells. This information will be used to develop high quality promotional 
resources for this aspect of the County’s Heritage in the longer term. 
In 2025, the aim was to create a community-based fact-finding process which would explore 
previously unrecorded memories, stories, traditions, customs, current use or non-use 
associated with the unique large number of tidal holy wells that occur in the South 
Conemara region and in particular their connection to St 
Colmcille.

pothole holy wells and their links to St. Colmcille.  The work
